# Graph `example_graph`

## When to use

Use it for questions about who works where, how the company is structured and who is
accountable for which process. Do not use it for contracts or payroll; those are not in the
graph.

## Is it available here?

Load the `graph-cli` skill as well before your first `graph` command: it has every command with its options, the change sets of `graph apply` and the error codes. The rules of working with `graph` below hold from the first call, with or without it.

Run `graph graphs --json`. Use this skill only if an item named `example_graph` is listed (title: Example graph). Pass `--graph example_graph` to every command, as the examples here do, so they work in every directory; a project whose pointer makes `example_graph` the default may leave it out.

Text values are written in the graph language `en`.

Working with `graph`:

- Run each call as a plain command that starts with `graph` and passes `--json` (the module views of `graph describe module` read better as text): no `cd`, variables, loops, pipes or heredocs, which a restricted harness refuses. If a call is refused, run it again in that form before you give up.
- Read the answer: `ok`, then `data`; on failure `error.hint` is the command to run next. Never cut an answer short; ask for less: `--fields <attr>,<attr>` on `find`, `get` and `neighbors`, or `graph query` with `RETURN` of just the columns you need (read the module first with `graph describe module <module> --graph example_graph`; `graph describe schema --module <module> --graph example_graph --compact --json` lists its patterns).
- Never guess an option, type, field, relation or state: `graph <command> --help` lists the options, `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json` the fields, states and relations.
- Preview `create`, `apply`, `transition`, `supersede` and `retract` with `--dry-run`, then run them without; one `update`, `link` or `unlink` may run directly. Say why in `--reason`, and pass `--expect <rev>` when the write depends on what you read. A change set for `graph apply` goes into a file in the working directory.
- Read `data.findings` of every write and tell the user about each warning.

## Subject areas

| Module | Prefix | What it holds | Types | Links to other modules |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `company` | `co` | The company as a whole, the main module that brings its subject areas together; it holds no terms of its own. | 0 | none |
| `operations` | `ops` | How work gets done, the processes, the guidelines that govern them and the training positions need; not who is in the structure. | 3 | `organization` (2 out, 0 in), `people` (0 out, 1 in) |
| `organization` | `org` | The structure of the company, its units, the positions in them and what they cost; not the people or the work done. | 5 | `operations` (0 out, 2 in), `people` (0 out, 1 in) |
| `people` | `ppl` | The people the company knows, who they are and how to reach them; not their positions or units. | 1 | `operations` (1 out, 0 in), `organization` (1 out, 0 in) |

Built-in modules, shared by every graph: `core`.

- Before you work in a module, read it: `graph describe module <module> --graph example_graph` lists its types, its relations, its links to and from other modules (with the other module named) and its rules. Read its text; `--json` is more than twice the size.
- To find a term whose module you do not know: `graph describe search <text> --graph example_graph --json` (types, relations, fields, enum values and states).
- For the fields, states and relations of one type: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.
- The same module views as text, and an index of every type with its module: [references/model.md](references/model.md) and the pages `references/modules/<module>.md`.

## Functions

This graph has no published functions.

## Names and ids

- Aliases such as `GUIDE-0001` (`ops:Guideline`) start with the prefix of the entity's type; the module pages list the prefix of every type, `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json` names it (`alias_prefix`). The number is zero-padded to 4 digits (`GUIDE-0001`, never `GUIDE-1`) and grows past 9999. A full id works everywhere; on the command line 8 or more trailing hex digits of it work too.
- `graph lookup <value> --graph example_graph --json` finds entities by name, ignoring case; it matches the name fields of a type, not other text. The module pages list them per type; `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json` marks them with `role` (`label`: main name; `alt_label`: other names; `hidden_label`: hidden names, matched but never shown).
- Names are not unique, so `lookup` returns candidates; `--for <relation>` or `--for <function>.<param>` keeps those that can fill that slot. Use the returned alias or id only when exactly one candidate matches exactly (`match.kind` is `exact`). With several, or only prefix matches, do not answer about one of them first: unless type and `facts` show which one the request means, list them with their names and ask which one is meant, then answer.
- `graph search <value> --graph example_graph --json` searches names and every text field, forgiving case, accents, typos and parts of words. Its results are suggestions: read one with `graph get` before you use it.
- Before you create an entity of a type with names, search for its name and its short forms. If one is the same thing, use it and add the new name to its other names field instead of creating another. When you create one, fill its other names fields with the abbreviations and synonyms people use. A write finding `data.semantic.possible_duplicate` names entities that already carry the name or a near spelling of it.

## Model

The modules and every type with its module and page: [references/model.md](references/model.md); one page per module in `references/modules/`. Fields, lifecycles and rules of a type, the live source, which wins when they differ: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.
